While `tempfile.path` in the current controller code is system-generated and safe, this method is a public class method (`OptimizedImage.downsize`, `OptimizedImage.resize`) that accepts arbitrary `from` and `to` paths. Any caller passing a user-controlled filename (e.g., an upload filename containing `; malicious_command` or `$(malicious_command)`) would result in shell command injection. The `instructions` array is built by joining strings with spaces, and paths are not quoted or escaped. For example, if `from` is `/tmp/upload; rm -rf /;.png`, the shell command becomes `convert /tmp/upload; rm -rf /;.png[0] ...` which executes `rm -rf /`. This is a critical security vulnerability if any code path passes user-controlled filenames to these methods. The current controller code uses `tempfile.path` (safe), but the method itself is unsafe by design. Consequence: arbitrary command execution if any caller passes untrusted input as file paths.

findings.title: Method overload ambiguity: two `downsize` methods with different arities may cause confusion
findings.body: The class now has two `self.downsize` methods: one at line 145 taking `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and one at line 149 taking `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Ruby resolves these by arity — 4 arguments (plus opts) vs 3 arguments (plus opts). The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)` which matches the 3-argument version (line 149). However, this overload pattern is fragile: if someone calls `downsize(from, to, 800, 600)` they get the first version which formats as "800x600"; if they call `downsize(from, to, "800x600")` they get the second version. The two methods have different semantics — one takes separate width/height, the other takes a dimension string. This is confusing API design. The original code had a single `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` that called `dimensions(width, height)` internally. The refactoring introduced this overload to support passing a percentage string directly, but it creates an inconsistent API. Consequence: potential bugs if callers mix up the calling conventions, and reduced code clarity.

findings.title: Downsize loop modifies tempfile in-place, but `content_type` variable may be undefined for URL-based uploads
findings.body: In the `create_upload` method, `content_type` is only assigned in the `else` branch (line 60: `content_type = file.content_type`). For API URL-based uploads (line 54-56), `content_type` is never assigned. The downsize loop on lines 64-70 runs for both branches (it only checks `tempfile` and `filename`). After the loop, line 72 calls `Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, content_type: content_type, ...)`. For URL-based uploads, `content_type` is `nil` (undefined local variable becomes nil in Ruby when referenced). This was the case before the change too, but the downsize loop now processes URL-based image uploads, potentially modifying the tempfile. If `Upload.create_for` uses `content_type` to determine how to process the file, passing `nil` for a downsized image could cause issues. Additionally, after in-place downsizing, the file's actual content type may change (e.g., ImageMagick might output a different format), but `content_type` remains whatever it was (or nil). Consequence: incorrect content type stored in the database, potential processing errors in `Upload.create_for` or downstream thumbnail generation.

findings.title: `tempfile.size` after in-place modification may be stale or incorrect, causing wrong filesize stored in Upload
findings.body: After the downsize loop modifies the tempfile in-place via ImageMagick, line 72 calls `Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, ...)`. The `tempfile.size` call returns the size of the file on disk at that moment. However, Ruby's `Tempfile` (and `File`) objects may cache file size or have buffered state. More critically, if ImageMagick's `convert` wrote to the same path, the file size on disk has changed, but if there are any file handles open or OS-level caching, `tempfile.size` might not reflect the actual current size. Additionally, `Upload.create_for` likely reads the file content and may compute its own size or SHA1 — if it uses the passed `tempfile.size` parameter for validation or storage, a stale or incorrect value could cause the upload to be rejected or stored with wrong metadata. The correct approach is to re-stat the file after modification or use a new tempfile. Consequence: incorrect file size stored in the `uploads` table, potential validation failures, and broken download/display of uploads.
